Structures
EXAMPLES
SWITCHING CLAUSES
Had + Past participle + by
Jake had already published his first book by the age of 20.
By the age of 20, Jake had already published his first book.
Had + Past participle + before
The boss had bitten everyone’s head off before I got with the answer.
before I got with the answer, the boss had bitten everyone’s head off.
Had + Past participle + when
Jazmin had already had a fit when HH.RR. solved the problem.
when HH.RR. solved the problem, Jazmin had already had a fit
.There is another way to use past perfect using If clauses to talk about unreal situations in the past:
If I had known, I would have told you. (Unit 45 will explained all about that)
When we work with past tense, we can also talk about things that had already happen or taken place before others. We use past perfect for tha.
slideDifferences.publishedText: Structures EXAMPLES SWITCHING CLAUSES Had + Past participle + by Jake had already published his first book by the age of 20. By the age of 20, Jake had already published his first book. Had + Past participle + before The boss had bitten everyone’s head off before I got with the answer. Before I got with the answer, the boss had bitten everyone’s head off. Had + Past participle + when Jazmin had already had a fit when HR solved the problem. When HR solved the problem, Jazmin had already had a fit. .There is another way to use past perfect using If clauses to talk about unreal situations in the past: If I had known, I would have told you. (Unit 45 will explain all about that). Past perfect can also be used in questions and negative sentences. When we work with past tense, we can also talk about things that had already happened or taken place before others. We use past perfect for that.

slideDifferences.nativeText:
To Consider 
1. Past Perfect + By uses normally a noun phrase after the preposition. 
2. Past Perfect + Before uses normally a clause in simple past after the 
    preposition. 
3. Past Perfect + When uses normally a clause in simple past after the 
    preposition.  
4. If we talk about one single event, there’s no need for us to use past perfect. E.G. Romans had spoken Latin. The correct form is: Romans spoke Latin.
5.  We can use a past perfect clause alone when the context is already known. E.G. 
Context: A mum asked by phone if her son did his homework.
                -Totally, Mrs. Swan. Jax had already done his homework when you called.

If we talk about one single event, there’s no need for us to use past perfect. Instead, we use simple past. E.G. Romans had spoken Latin. The correct form is: Romans spoke Latin. 5. We can use a past perfect clause alone when the context is already known. E.G. Context: A mum asked by phone if her son did his homework. -Totally, Mrs. Swan. Jax had already done his homework when you called.

C. Read the following paragraph and extract sentences with the delexical verbs and tell your teacher what is their intended meaning.
What a day!

Hi, have you ever had one of those days when everything seemed to go wrong? I'm sure you have, I know I have. I remember one particular day, I'd been invited to a party and there was someone going who I'd never met but I really wanted to meet, so I was quite excited about going to this party, and I maybe spent too long getting ready and I was a bit late when I was leaving the house, but not too late. But then I looked down and saw I had a hole in my tights! So I had to go back inside, change my tights, come out again, so I was getting a little bit late for the party, but not too bad. I got in my car, started driving, about halfway to the party my car stopped. 

I couldn't understand what was the matter until I looked at the petrol gauge: it had run out of petrol! Why? Because I'd lent my car to my son the day before and he'd used the petrol and he hadn't filled the car up! So I thought I'd ring the AA. I looked in my handbag to find my mobile phone, but I couldn't find it. Why? Because I'd left it next to my bed charging. So even though it was pouring with rain, I had to get out of my car, in my party clothes, walk to the petrol station and come back with petrol. 

By which time I was nearly 2 hours late. So, I was so flustered about being late, I started to drive and I just took a wrong turn and I ended up on this one-way system, totally lost, driving round and round for at least 45 minutes before I managed to get my bearings. So finally, I arrived at the party over 3 hours late and when I arrived the person I wanted to meet had just left, all the food had gone, and my host was horribly drunk. I was so disappointed that I just turned around and left and went back home. Have you ever had a terrible day like that, when everything went wrong? If you have, write and tell us about it.

texts: IDIOM
MEANING
EXAMPLE
GO BALLISTIC
To lose one’s temper by shooting words.
My dad went ballistic when he found out we had a party in the house.
MAKE SOMEONE LIVID
To get someone  really furious
Then, I knew she had just made me livid.
BLOW SOMEONE’S TOP
To become very angry about something.
My dad just blew my mum’s top when she knew he had not paid the hall for the party.
TO BE CROSS WITH
To be angry at someone.
I am just cross with her now!
TO BITE SOMEONE’S HEAD OFF
To reply sharply and brusquely to someone.
The teacher just bit all students’ heads for the problem they caused.
TO FLY OFF THE HANDLE
To describe a person that suddenly gets really angry.
Every time someone talks about the changes in the school policy, Jessica flies off the handle.
TO HAVE A FIT
To become very upset
Don’t have a fit, please!
TO BLOW A GASKET
To lose one’s temper.
If the boss comes back and we aren’t done with this, he is going to blow a gasket.
Look at the phrases and  discuss them with your teacher. Did you know them?

When we work with past tense, we can also talk about things that had already happened or taken place before others. We use past perfect for that.

texts: To Consider
1. Past Perfect + By uses normally a noun phrase after the preposition.
2. Past Perfect + Before uses normally a clause in simple past after the
preposition.
3. Past Perfect + When uses normally a clause in simple past after the
preposition.
4. If we talk about one single event, there’s no need for us to use past perfect. E.G. Romans had spoken Latin. The correct form is: Romans spoke Latin.

5.  We can use a past perfect clause alone when the context is already known. E.G. 
Context: A mum asked by phone if her son did his homework.
-Totally, Mrs. Swan. Jax had already done his homework when you called.

texts: We can use past perfect to talk about the following aspects.
Functions
Examples
Express actions that time up to a point in the past.
They had already moved three times by the end of 2020.
Talk about undone or incomplete actions in the past.
Before he went ballistic, I had delivered what he wanted.
State actions that already happened before others in the past.
When the police came into the building, The gang had already stolen everything.
To consider
In most cases, already can be the adverb to use; however, ever and never can suit depending on the context.

texts: C. Read the following paragraph and extract sentences with the delexical verbs and tell your teacher what is their intended meaning.
What a day!

Hi, have you ever had one of those days when everything seemed to go wrong? I'm sure you have, I know I have. I remember one particular day, I'd been invited to a party and there was someone going who I'd never met but I really wanted to meet, so I was quite excited about going to this party, and I maybe spent too long getting ready and I was a bit late when I was leaving the house, but not too late. But then I looked down and saw I had a hole in my tights! So I had to go back inside, change my tights, come out again, so I was getting a little bit late for the party, but not too bad. I got in my car, started driving, about halfway to the party my car stopped.

I couldn't understand what was the matter until I looked at the petrol gauge: it had run out of petrol! Why? Because I'd lent my car to my son the day before and he'd used the petrol and he hadn't filled the car up! So I thought I'd ring the AA. I looked in my handbag to find my mobile phone, but I couldn't find it. Why? Because I'd left it next to my bed charging. So even though it was pouring with rain, I had to get out of my car, in my party clothes, walk to the petrol station and come back with petrol.

By which time I was nearly 2 hours late. So, I was so flustered about being late, I started to drive and I just took a wrong turn and I ended up on this one-way system, totally lost, driving round and round for at least 45 minutes before I managed to get my bearings. So finally, I arrived at the party over 3 hours late and when I arrived the person I wanted to meet had just left, all the food had gone, and my host was horribly drunk. I was so disappointed that I just turned around and left and went back home. Have you ever had a terrible day like that, when everything went wrong? If you have, write and tell us about it.
